extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and poets (readers interested in descriptive/poetic technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing vivid imagery and affecting descriptions in poetry and prose, including advice on what pleases the imagination (greatness, beauty, strangeness), how to cultivate imagination, and how to handle fantastical or architectural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour nature; avoid rigid artificiality in plantations/gardens
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers (and garden designers, by analogy) should not lay out plantations 'by the Rule and Line'; natural-looking arrangement and concealment of art pleases the imagination more than trees cut into 'Mathematical Figure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the luxuriancy and diffusion of boughs to geometrical trimming: 'I would rather look upon a Tree in all its Luxuriancy and Diffusion of Boughs and Branches, than when it is thus cut and trimmed into a Mathematical Figure'; an 'Orchard in Flower' is 'infinitely more delightful' than an over-finished parterre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance utility and beauty in landscape/setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plantations and improvements should serve both profit and pleasure—turning marshes or mountains into planted, useful, and beautiful parts of an estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how 'a Marsh overgrown with Willows, or a Mountain shaded with Oaks, are not only more beautiful, but more beneficial'—combine ornament and usefulness when composing scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish greatness of bulk from greatness of manner in architecture/scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness may relate to sheer bulk/size or to the manner in which something is built or presented; manner can make a small work produce nobler ideas than a much larger but meanly executed one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small structure with majestic manner may affect the imagination more than a huge one of ordinary manner: compare the Pantheon with a Gothic cathedral—the 'Greatness of the Manner' is decisive for the spectator's feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of manner: few principal members and bold, ample relief
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce grandeur of manner, divide principal members into few parts which are all great, with bold and ample relievo; avoid many small intermingled particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Monsieur Freart observes: keep principal members few and 'all great and of a bold and ample Relievo'; remove 'ordinary Confusion' produced by many small cavities and quarter rounds that 'produce no Effect in great and massy Works' and scatter the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concave/convex and round forms to produce a unified, impressive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures like the concave and convex, round pillars, vaulted roofs and domes have a greater air and strike the imagination because the eye can take in more of the body at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms where the sight grasps the whole idea at once (domes, arches) rather than figures (square pillars) that force the eye to move over separate sides; 'the entire Concavity falls into your Eye at once.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Words can give more lively ideas than sight; use description to heighten nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-chosen words often paint a scene more vividly than direct sight: the poet can 'get the better of Nature' by selecting, heightening, or enlarging parts of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description lets the poet 'give us as free a View of it as he pleases'—present complex or emphasized parts that the actual view might not show; choose expressions that raise stronger, more complex ideas than the eye alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary pleasure: the delight of comparing words with originals
rubrics_metrics.description: One source of pleasure is the mind's act of comparing ideas raised by words (or pictures/statues) with ideas from original objects; this 'comparison' operation itself yields enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle explains enjoyment of statuary, painting, description, mimickry, and many forms of wit; even disagreeable objects (a dunghill) can please when the description exhibits aptness and the operation of comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness of expression: make descriptions suitable to the object
rubrics_metrics.description: A description is pleasing when its expressions are apt to excite the intended image—expressive, significant words that accurately clothe the idea increase pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure sometimes is more 'of the Understanding than of the Fancy'—focus on the 'Aptness of the Description to excite the Image'; craft phrasings that precisely trigger the relevant set of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate imagination and the force of words
rubrics_metrics.description: To form accurate judgments of descriptions and to write effectively, a writer must have a naturally lively imagination and must 'have well weighed the Force and Energy' of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop both a warm, retentive fancy and the judgment to know which expressions are most significant and what strength they gain from combination; 'A Poet should take as much Pains in forming his Imagination, as a Philosopher in cultivating his Understanding.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden experience in nature and the arts to enrich imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should be thoroughly conversant with country life, court pomp, painting, statuary, architecture (both existing and ruined) to supply material for varied and powerful imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire images from 'the Pomp and Magnificence of courts' as well as 'Country Images'; study great exemplars—Homer (great/sublime), Virgil (beautiful), Ovid (strange), and Milton (combines these arts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the poetic model to achieve desired imaginative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Different masters produce different effects—Homer hits the sublime and great, Virgil the beautiful and orderly, Ovid the strange—so select models according to intended tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you aim for sublimity and massed grandeur, emulate Homer; for harmonious beauty, Virgil; for novelty and the marvellous, Ovid; Milton exemplifies mastery across kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make terror and pity pleasurable by preserving distance/safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of terror or grief can be pleasurable because readers can reflect on their own safety; the objects are 'Dreadful and Harmless' when presented as past or fictitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use terror productively, maintain fictional or temporal distance so the reader can 'consider them as Dreadful and Harmless' and thus derive the secret pleasure from reflection on their own condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy-way / supernatural writing requires a special imaginative cast and altered speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing about beings with no real pattern (fairies, witches, spirits) is difficult and needs an imagination naturally fertile and superstitious, plus knowledge of legends and antiquated romances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making supernatural beings speak like ordinary people; their 'Sense ought to be a little discoloured' so their manners and speech be proper to their otherness; draw on childhood traditions and nurse-tales to 'humour those Notions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic licence: improve and combine nature, but avoid absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may 'mend and perfect Nature'—e.g., combine features of different seasons or climates to produce stronger scenes—but must not 'reform her too much, and run into Absurdities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may merge flowers of several seasons, invent richer species, or rearrange rivers for delight; constantly check that imaginative improvement remains plausible within the poem's own logic to avoid absurd effects.
